primary.thesis: As of late May 2026, the FOMC holds the target range at 3.50-3.75%. It paused after three cuts in late 2025 and has kept rates there through the spring. The mechanism favours another hold at the July 28-29 meeting. Core inflation is still above target and tariff pass-through is keeping goods prices firm. Unemployment is drifting up only slowly, not breaking. The chair handover from Powell (term ended May 2026) to a successor who leans toward cuts means the new chair's first meetings will likely be spent building committee consensus rather than forcing an early move against hawkish regional presidents. A July cut would need a clear labour-market break in the June and July data, which is not the base case. A hike is implausible with a new chair who favours cuts and a softening labour market. Emergency or 50bp moves in either direction would need a crisis.

basket.reason: Core expression: inflation above target, no labour shock yet, and a new chair still building consensus all point to a hold.
A 50bp+ cut needs a financial or labour crisis that is not visible as of late May.
A 50bp+ hike is essentially off the table under a new chair who favours cuts and a softening labour market.
The committee's bias is toward easing or holding, not hiking. Tariff inflation is being treated as a one-time price-level effect.

failure_narrative: The basket mainly loses if the Fed cuts 25bp in July. The path: the June and July payroll reports come in weak or negative, unemployment rises toward 4.7-5%, and jobless claims climb. At the same time, core PCE cools as tariff effects fade. The new chair then uses his first months to argue for 'normalising' rates lower, backed by the governors appointed by the administration and by dovish regional presidents, and the committee delivers a cut (possibly signalled at the June meeting). A lesser failure mode is a sudden credit or market event (private-credit stress, bank funding strain) that forces a 50bp cut. A hike would require an inflation re-acceleration, for example from an oil shock, which is the least likely path.
hedge_thesis: In the worlds where the Fed cuts in July, US growth and labour data have weakened and policy has turned dovish. The same mechanism shows up outside the FOMC decision itself. Weaker US data and a lower expected policy path push short-dated Treasury yields down and flatten or steepen the curve from the front end. They also weaken the dollar against the yen and euro, because rate differentials narrow, and lift gold, because real yields fall and the Fed is seen as less independent under a politically aligned chair. So a thesis that 2-year Treasury yields fall and gold and the yen strengthen through July 2026 tends to be true exactly when the hold thesis fails. It also pays in the growth-scare version of the failure (rising unemployment, higher recession odds).
